newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket launches new series INTELSAT satellite.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches new series INTELSAT satellite.

text.p: Western Europe's 94th Ariane rocket blasted off from equatorial French Guiana on Friday and placed into orbit the first of a new series of satellites for INTELSAT.

The Ariane 44P rocket equipped with four solid strap-on boosters lifted off at 10:07 p.m. local time (0107 GMT Saturday) into a cloudy equatorial night sky from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch center in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
The launch was delayed for over an hour because of heavy ground winds.
Twenty minutes later space officials said the INTELSAT 801 satellite separated from the Ariane rocket.

The Washington-based International Telecommunications Satellite Organization (INTELSAT) said INTELSAT 801 is the first of the INTELSAT-8 series -- a run of six satellites with more capacity than the previous INTELSAT-7 family. The satellite will service the Indian Ocean region.
"The mission of INTELSAT-8 is a classic mission of INTELSAT: telephone, data transmission and television," Claude Burgio, INTELSAT vice president for engineering, told Reuters.

INTELSAT, with 140 member nations, owns and operates 24 satellites and remains the world's major operator of international satellite services despite recent competition from private non-governmental providers. The organization said 1996 revenues exceeded $911 million.

The 3.4 tonne satellite was built by Lockheed Martin Astro Space in New Jersey. It will have the capacity to provide up to 112,500 two-way telephone circuits using digital multiplication equipment and four television channels.
INTELSAT'S first satellite, Early Bird launched in 1965, was the world's first commercial telecommunications satellite. It carried 360 telephone circuits.
The Paris-based Arianespace company which launches the Ariane-4 rocket series controls more than half the world's commercial rocket launch market.

It has successfully placed 18 heavy satellites into orbit aboard 12 Ariane-4 rockets since January 1996. The company said it now has firm orders to launch 39 satellites worth an estimated $3.3 billion.
But on June 4, the first more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in a major setback for the European space program.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over operations of Ariane-5 early this year, but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is planned for July at earliest.
